entries.title: A Biotech Founder Makes the Moral Case for Gene-Editing Human Embryos
entries.summary: The practice of editing the genes of embryos remains highly controversial and risky, but Origin Genomics founder Cathy Tie argues its a “moral imperative” to address hereditary diseases.
entries.content:
When the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced in 2018 that he had created the first gene-edited babies, the experiment was widely condemned as reckless and premature. It ended with He in prison.

But that hasn’t stopped the push for gene-edited human embryos, with biotech entrepreneur Cathy Tie arguing that doing so isn’t just urgent—it’s a “moral imperative.”

Tie is the 30-year-old founder of Origin Genomics, a company that launched in March with plans to bring gene-edited embryos to IVF clinics. In a new commentary published in the journal Trends in Genetics, she argues for public funding and new regulatory pathways to advance gene-edited babies and eventually move into clinical use.

But questions remain about what evidence researchers will need to determine whether gene-edited embryos are safe enough to attempt a human pregnancy—and what risks might remain for the resulting children.

“There are cautionary tales of first human trials where there was really no flashing red light, and people died,” says Hank Greely, a law professor and director of the Center for Law and the Biosciences at Stanford University.

So-called germ-line gene editing involves modifying cells involved in human reproduction, like embryos. Any changes made could be passed on to future generations. That could mean, for example, correcting a devastating genetic mutation for good. But accidental DNA edits elsewhere, known as “off-target effects,” could introduce new health risks that could also be passed down. Those high stakes are part of why dozens of countries have banned gene-editing of human embryos intended for pregnancy.

People at risk of passing a genetic disease on to their children can use IVF combined with genetic screening to identify disease-free embryos before transfer to the womb. Critics of embryo editing argue that screening tools make the need for it very small. Gene-editing embryos, Greely says, would be helping “a fraction of a fraction of a fraction.”

The drawback of the current approach is that IVF is inefficient; viable embryos can be hard to come by, even for people without an inherited disease risk. Ian Watts and Cheyenne Ziegler, for example, underwent three rounds of IVF in their attempt to have children that do not carry the genetic variant responsible for Watts’ Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, a degenerative neurological disorder that impacts fine motor skills and mobility. With any IVF cycle, eggs regularly don’t fertilize, and those that do often stall in development or have chromosomal abnormalities. Adding additional screening for disease means that some viable embryos also don’t make the cut.

In Watts and Ziegler’s case, three rounds of IVF have produced eight chromosomally normal embryos, but only three without Watts’ variant. Those three embryos are likely not enough to give the couple the three or four children they hope to have one day.

“The choices currently available are either not having children or doing lots of IVF,” says Watts, a 36-year-old engineer in Long Beach, California. Gene editing could give people like him more chances at a future family. It could also help couples in the extremely rare situation where every embryo would inherit a disease-causing mutation, such as partners who each have two copies of a harmful variant.

“We’re here to treat these diseases, not just exclude embryos and call it a day,” says Tie, a former Thiel fellow who’s alluded to herself as “biotech Barbie.”

The invention of CRISPR raised the possibility of gene-edited babies more than a decade ago, and newer forms of gene editing offer increasing precision. In June, researchers at Columbia University revealed that they had edited early-stage human embryos using a technique called base editing with incredible accuracy. Tie cites this work in her commentary, arguing that precision editing is now well within reach.

If medicine can safely and effectively prevent a disease, she writes, deciding whether to use that treatment should be part of a patient’s reproductive choice. “The obligation of medicine is not only to avoid causing harm but also to prevent avoidable suffering when effective interventions exist,” she writes. Tie says, though, the technology shouldn’t to enhance traits such as intelligence.

And people seem to want the choice: A European survey released in July found that more people supported than opposed human embryo editing.

Tie says that New York City–based Origin is currently working on “optimizing” base- and prime-editing tools on human embryos that IVF patients have donated for research. (The company is currently only testing it in human embryonic stem cell lines.) She expects the company to have significant data in the coming months showing that its embryo-editing tools are safe and efficient. Tie’s first human embryo-editing company, Manhattan Genomics, abruptly shuttered this year after operating for only a few months.

But while the Columbia work demonstrated that precise genetic changes to human embryos are possible, the researchers didn’t correct disease-causing mutations. Some of the editing tools they developed also resulted in unwanted and inconsistent genomic changes, leading them to conclude in a paper published this month that “undesirable consequences” meant the technology was not ready for clinical use.

Variability also means that one editor working doesn’t establish that another will be safe.

“Each and every mutation will therefore be a new medicine,” says Dieter Egli, who led the Columbia work. On top of the added technical challenges, that could make embryo-editing especially time-consuming and expensive to develop.

Tie is clear that she does not think embryo editing is ready for human patients, but she argues it’s close enough that it’s time to address the legal and funding barriers that stand in the way of developing it for use in US clinics. Federal funding for human embryo research is currently legally restricted, and the Food and Drug Administration is barred from considering clinical trials involving embryos with heritable genetic modifications.

Many scientists working on embryo editing believe it will one day come to clinics. Where they differ is when and what it will take to establish it as safe enough.

Doing so, says Paula Amato, a professor of ob-gyn at Oregon Health & Science University who also advises gene-editing company Preventive, will require rigorous assessment of embryos in the lab before moving to trials in nonhuman primates. Those studies should also follow several generations to make sure there are no unexpected changes. Origin, though, is not currently working with animal models, nor does it have immediate plans to do so.

But even with an editing tool that appears to perform perfectly in studies, it will be impossible to ensure that any embryo implanted in a human is free of unintended genetic changes. Before transfer, edited embryos would likely undergo genetic testing. Embryo biopsies sample only a few cells, though, which may not reflect whether different cells carry different genetic changes.

Undetected off-target effects could manifest years later, after a gene-edited baby has grown up and had children of their own.

“You can never be sure that you did your homework,” says Shoukhrat Mitalipov, director of the Center for Embryonic Cell and Gene Therapy at OHSU. “You think that it's safe, but you’re transferring a kind of black box.” (Mitalipov advised Manhattan Genomics.)

Patients, Amato says, will have to be counseled on these risks.

Watts and Ziegler say that the risks of a novel technology would be worth it for the chance of giving one of their affected embryos a disease-free life. Ziegler is currently 20 weeks pregnant with one of their unaffected embryos, but they have continued to hold on to the ones with Watts’ variant in hopes that correcting them will be an option one day.

“If the choices are to discard or to give a new technology a chance, I would lean toward giving new technology a chance,” Ziegler says.

entries.title: The Best Gifts for Book Lovers (2026): E-Readers, Handy Accessories, Book Sets
entries.summary: Any one of these gift ideas will make your favorite bookworm very happy, from e-readers and accessories to handy reading essentials.
entries.content:
I love losing myself in a good book, and I’m not the only one. Finding great gifts for book lovers isn’t just about testing for the best e-reader (which we have!) or rounding up all the accessories worth adding to your Kindle (we’ve done that too), but rather it’s about setting up your favorite reader to keep enjoying stories.

You can help them with anything from a new reading gadget or a handy accessory to cozy items to settle in for a nice, long reading session. After all, if there’s anything we’ve learned from the rise of #BookTok, it’s that there’s no lack of accessories and items that can make a reader happier than ever. Here are our favorite gifts for book lovers we’re shopping this season.

Be sure also to check out our other buying guides, including Best Kindles, Best E-Readers, Best Kindle Accessories, and Best Digital Notebooks. If you’re on the hunt for more gifts, don’t miss the rest of our gift guides.

Updated September 2026: This guide has been refreshed with current prices and gift ideas, including the PopSockets Dragon Sterling case, Lamicall tablet stands, Ikea Kajplats smart bulb, and two LED devices to use while you read.

Featured Gifts

A New E-Reader

When I got back into reading, I fell in love with ebooks and getting free copies from the library that I would read on my Libby app. That year, for my birthday, I was gifted a Kindle from two different people, and I’ve never looked back. Whether they’re a new reader looking for a better way to read or one who’s complaining about how heavy their books are, an e-reader makes for a great solution (and you can still get those free library books on it!).

E-Reader Accessories

From cute cases to handy straps that make reading easier, there’s no lack of fun options to add to a Kindle or other e-readers.

Other Reader Gadgets

There are lots of little gadgets that can improve your reading, and these are some of my favorites.

Book Bags

If the book lover in your life is known for toting their e-reader or book of choice everywhere they go, here are some fun accessories for carrying them around (and for logging their thoughts as they read!).

Stickers, Journals, and Annotation Tools

Whether they’re looking to decorate their e-reader or the pages of their books, there’s a fun add-on here for every kind of reader.

Reading Vibes

Gifts for your loca l book lover don’t have to be books and book items. Help them set the mood while they read with these cozy gift ideas.

Gorgeous Books and Boxed Sets

Looking to give the gift of a true book? These box sets and illustrated editions are worth collecting.

Book Subscriptions

Buying a book for someone can be hard if you’re not sure what they’re into or what they’ve already read. But covering a few months of a subscription is the gift that gives over and over again.

entries.title: The Best Gaming Routers (2026): Tested By a Family of Gamers
entries.summary: Gaming online can seriously strain your internet connection, but the best gaming routers could give you the edge.
entries.content:
Few things are more frustrating than packet loss or high ping causing in-game lag. It always seems to happen at the worst possible moment, when you’re about to snipe an unsuspecting opponent or screech into a hairpin bend. While there are other potential causes, your substandard router could be doing you dirty. The best gaming routers promise rock solid connections and can usually prioritize game-related traffic to reduce the risk of issues. They also frequently feature fancy designs and customizable lighting to fit your gaming room.

Now, you don’t necessarily need a special gaming router. A good router is a good router, and you’ll find tons of them in my guides to the Best Routers and Best Mesh Systems. You can also get a better connection simply by running an Ethernet cable from your router to your gaming PC. That said, I have tested several gaming routers, and my top pick is the fastest router I have ever tested.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Asus Gaming Routers

The brand I recommend as the best for gamers is Asus. The Taiwanese company has a long gaming history and dedicated sub-brands like Republic of Gamers (ROG). It produces fast, highly configurable routers with free security software and many gaming extras. Ports are usually generous, there’s no need for a subscription, and you can combine different Asus routers that support AiMesh into a mesh system to extend your coverage. The potential downsides are the relatively high prices, occasionally buggy firmware, and the need to dig into configuration settings to get the best performance.

Topping my testing charts, the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BE98 Pro is a supremely capable, quad-band Wi-Fi 7 gaming router. In terms of raw speed, this is the best router I have tested to date. That alone makes it feel worthy of the “gimmick” of being designed explicitly for gaming. It is very similar to the RT-BE96U in my regular router guide, but with the ROG model, Asus has added a second 6-GHz band on top of the existing 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands. This massively increases the available bandwidth, affording you plenty of space for multiple gaming streams, or giving you an extra band for wireless backhaul if you decide to set up a mesh using Asus’ AiMesh connectivity. It also has an extra 10-Gbps LAN port, giving you one 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, two 10-Gbps LAN, four Gigabit LAN, one USB 3.2, and a USB 2.0 port. The USB ports come in handy for NAS devices. You must pay extra for these additions, so if you don’t have multiple gaming streams or a NAS, you can save money with the RT-BE96U and still get great performance.

This is also easily the biggest router I have ever tested at nearly 14 inches across, with eight huge antennas, and it weighs 4.4 pounds. It is far from subtle, won’t blend in, and could prove tricky to place due to its size. Because it’s a gaming router, Asus has included Aura RGB lighting, so you can pick the colored lighting you want and make it a feature.

AiProtection Pro security software and parental controls, powered by Trend Micro, are bundled into the cost. This comprehensive security combo includes a firewall, intrusion prevention, malicious site blocking, automatic updates, and more. Parental controls include scheduling, website filtering by age, and usage stats. You also get VPN support with the option to connect remotely when you are out and about. You can redeem a free year of NordVPN service with this router. Naturally, there are some gaming-focused features, with game acceleration enabling you to prioritize gaming-related traffic through ports and packet analysis. If you have Asus’ ROG gear, it can be prioritized with a click, and Asus includes server acceleration to minimize latency through the third-party WTFast service.

Apart from the size and cost, there isn’t much to complain about here, but it is worth considering that the range on the 6-GHz band is limited and struggles to penetrate through walls, so you will need Wi-Fi 7 devices nearby to take full advantage of this router. Ideally, have it in the same room as your gaming PC or laptop. This router was originally touted to get Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) support, but it never did (look at the next pick if that’s something you want).

Asus ROG Strix GS-BE12000 for $400: If you don’t want to spend as much, but you’re set on a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router, and you want lots of ports, this model could make sense. I found it stable and seriously speedy on the 6-GHz and 5-GHz bands. It boasts 320 MHz channels on the 6-GHz band, Multi-Link Operation (MLO), and 4K-QAM (read my How to Buy a Router and Wi-Fi 7 guides for a breakdown on these terms). It has a 2.5 Gbps WAN and seven 2.5 Gbps LAN ports, two of which are dedicated gaming ports, and a USB 3.2 Gen 1 port. You get mostly the same excellent software and gaming options as my top pick. This is a scaled down version of the BE18000 ($530), and has 2 x 2 MIMO on the 6-GHz band instead of 4 x 4, but I think it’s a better buy for most folks, especially if you see it on sale. It’s worth noting that both models have official Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) support, which extends the range of the 6-GHz band to make it more comparable to the 5-GHz band range. I can’t test this here in the UK, as it’s only available in North America and requires your precise real-world location so local regulators can authorize it.

Asus TUF Gaming BE9400 for $265: The cheaper end of Asus gaming routers, this model is still a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router, and it doesn’t make too many compromises. It has one 2.5 Gbps WAN, three 2.5 Gbps LAN ports, and a USB 3.2 Gen 1 port. You miss out on some ROG-exclusive gaming features, the design is not as nice, and it lacks RGB lighting. But this router performed far better than the price would suggest, keeping pace with my top pick at close range, though coverage doesn’t extend as far.

Asus ROG Rapture GT6 (2-Pack) for $350: This Wi-Fi 6 system is a solid gaming mesh. Aside from the look, Asus touts game modes that boost performance and prioritize related traffic. My 2-pack of black routers (they come in white too) was simple to set up, and each sports a 2.5-Gbps WAN port, three Gigabit LAN ports, and a USB 3.2 Gen 1 port. The tri-band Asus ROG Rapture GT6 finished in the top half of the table in most tests. It has a single 2.4-GHz band and two 5-GHz bands (one is used for backhaul unless you connect the routers with an Ethernet cable). While the 2.4-GHz band performance was very good, the 5-GHz results were among the best I have recorded, and this system supports the wider 160-MHz channels and WPA3 for security. You also get AiProtection security software and comprehensive parental controls free for the lifetime of the product. The GT6 has VPN support, too, and you can use it as a VPN server when you are out. If your gaming rig doesn’t have Wi-Fi 7 yet and you need a mesh system for your home, this is worth a look.

Best TP-Link Gaming Routers

You can sometimes get a little more for your money with TP-Link, and it offers a dedicated gaming line-up under the Archer brand (prefaced with GE), but I don’t think they always offer the best value for performance compared to its regular Archer routers. Folks in the US may also hesitate because TP-Link has not yet secured a Conditional Approval from the FCC’s router ban (Asus and Netgear have). All routers that were already on sale (including everything here) are unaffected by the ban and software updates have a waiver at least until January 1, 2029. There’s a slim risk the waiver doesn’t get extended, but it’s unlikely (read my guide for more information).

This stunning tri-band Wi-Fi 7 gaming router features an angled design with customizable RGB lighting that screams Vader’s castle but also provides room for antennas to ensure extremely fast performance across the board. You also get a 10-Gbps port for your incoming internet connection, a further two 10-Gbps and four 2.5-Gbps Ethernet LAN ports, and a USB 3.0 port. The Tether app is solid, with some gaming-specific options, but separate subscriptions are required for extra security and parental controls. Despite the blazing fast results, the GE800 couldn’t quite match my top Wi-Fi 7 gaming pick above on the 6-GHz band, and it produced quite a lot of heat and audible fan noise. The upside is that it’s significantly cheaper.

TP-Link Archer GE400 (BE6500) for $220: This dual-band Wi-Fi 7 gaming router is a solid performer. At close range on the 5-GHz band, it can go toe-to-toe with most of the best routers. It also offers dedicated gaming features, though some of them require subscriptions. I was disappointed by the limited range, and the comparable TP-Link Archer BE400 (BE6500) ($180) is currently on sale for less. You also don’t have to spend much more to get the far superior, tri-band Archer BE600 (BE9700) ($250), giving you the full 6-GHz Wi-Fi 7 experience. For gamers who live alone in apartments or small homes, this router could still be a decent buy.

Other Gaming Routers I’ve Tested and Liked

Netgear used to manufacture dedicated gaming routers under the Nighthawk brand, but the latest Nighthawk routers are billed more as mainstream products (you’ll find a few in my Best Routers guide).

Netgear Nighthawk RAXE300 for $285: This Wi-Fi 6E gaming router has a curvy spaceship design in matte black with wings containing antennas for a strong signal throughout your home. The Nighthawk RAXE300 is a tri-band router with 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands. It served seamless, speedy Wi-Fi during two weeks of testing, with no issues handling a mix of four simultaneous gaming and video streams. A single 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN port, five gigabit LAN ports, and a USB-C 3.0 port will be enough for most folks.

The Nighthawk app is excellent and offers band splitting, guest network options, and a host of analytical tools. While both the Premium Smart Parental Controls ($8/month or $70/year) and Netgear Armor ($100/year) are slick, the extra expense is hard to swallow when many competitors offer cheaper or free alternatives with similar features. This is discontinued, but a few places still have new stock, and it’s still a great router.

Gaming Routers I Don’t Recommend

Here are a couple of gaming routers I tested that I don’t recommend.

Acer Predator Connect T7: Another brand with gaming pedigree, I had high hopes for this Acer system, but my excitement was short-lived because the half-baked Predator Connect T7 is a mess. Buggy installation, with the firmware update repeatedly failing, followed by flaky performance with frequent dropouts, made testing this system a frustrating experience. The band steering is poor and frequently dumped me onto the slowest 2.4-GHz band. The T7 also dropped my connection multiple times a day, froze video calls, and was a general pain.

MSI RadiX AXE6600: This Wi-Fi 6E tri-band gaming router has that familiar red and black Sith spider look, though you can customize the lighting. It proved very fast in most of my tests, coming close to the top of the table at short range on the 6-GHz band and offering average performance on the 5-GHz and 2.4-GHz bands. But the mobile app had limited options, a confusing layout, and was buggy (it crashed on me more than once). The web interface was better, with more options, including open VPN, simple parental controls, a guest network, and QoS optimization for gaming. Unfortunately, performance was inconsistent, and I suffered random drops twice in a week of testing.

Do I Need a Gaming Router?

The short answer is no. As I said in the intro, a good router is a good router, and you’ll find loads of great options that offer top-notch gaming performance in my Best Routers and Best Mesh Systems guides. That said, gaming routers do sometimes offer specific gaming features to help you prioritize gaming traffic, boost the speed of gaming streams, and keep lag to a minimum, though some of these features are available on regular routers, too. Gaming routers also sometimes have RGB lighting and designs that are supposed to appeal to gamers, though your mileage may vary.

Can I Add Routers or Extenders to Make a Mesh?

Many manufacturers allow you to create a mesh network by adding more routers or devices like Wi-Fi extenders, but check what is supported before you buy. For example, Asus AiMesh enables you to link multiple routers, while TP-Link’s OneMesh only allows you to add power-line adapters or range extenders. EasyMesh is a standard certification by the Wi-Fi Alliance that hopes to allow the mixing and matching of devices from different manufacturers to form a mesh, but few devices support it so far. You can also buy single mesh routers, like an Amazon Eero, and then add more later if you find that you need them. Based on my testing, a mesh is always better than an extender.

How Do Ethernet Cables Compare?

Running an Ethernet cable to create a wired connection between your home router and gaming PC or other device will always provide a faster, more stable, and more secure link than Wi-Fi. But running Ethernet cables everywhere can be messy. Read my Ethernet guide to learn more. Wireless connectivity makes life easy and is fast enough for most tasks.

How I Test Routers

To find the best gaming routers, I use each one for at least a week (usually longer) in a busy family home of four with lots of video streaming, gaming, and video calls. I also test the mobile apps and web interfaces to see how easy it is to change settings, set up parental controls, and access security features. My priority is to learn how well the router works in real-life rather than a lab, but I do also run a set of standardized tests, so that I have numbers to compare.

I run speed tests (downloads and uploads). I transfer files on the network on multiple devices (including iPhones, Android phones, Windows PCs, and MacBooks) from different spots around my home. I use NetSpot to survey signal strength throughout the house and create heat maps for comparison. I run the TamoSoft Throughput Test. I turn the power and modem off and on to find out how each system recovers.

entries.title: Black Twitter Is Thriving—on Threads
entries.summary: From outrage over Nolan Wells’ death to analysis of HBO Max’s Lanterns, Threads has transformed into a vital artery of the Black social media ecosystem.
entries.content:
Last week, after a Mississippi grand jury declined to bring criminal charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the 18-year-old Black college student who disappeared on Horn Island while traveling with a group of white friends and was later found dead, Black users on Threads demanded justice.

“Just so it’s abundantly clear: The state of Mississippi is covering up the murder of Nolan Wells,” user @_taexoxo posted two days after the September 21 decision. The case has incited racial tensions nationwide.

“This year a grand jury handed down an indictment for a pool of water turning green, but didn’t indict when a black kid was found floating face down in water!” commented comedian D.L. Hughley.

Black Americans have never shied away from calling out America’s racial hypocrisies—Twitter served as an indispensable tool as the Black Lives Matter movement swelled in the 2020s—but the chatter on Threads was uniquely charged for Wells. It was the latest bit of evidence showing that the platform has emerged as a vital artery of the Black social media ecosystem, at times even rivaling the influence Black Twitter once personified.

In 2021, when I first explored the cultural expansiveness of Black Twitter, I wrote that it was “all the things: news and analysis, call and response, judge and jury—a comedy showcase, therapy session, and family cookout all in one.” Five years later, Threads is proving to be its spiritual successor, a robust digital universe where no conversation, no matter how ugly or awkward, is off limits.

As with Black Twitter, on Threads you are just as likely to come across conversations around the ageism double standard that Black women face as you are off-the-cuff TV commentary. Speaking of HBO Max’s new superhero thriller, Lanterns, one user recently quipped that it’s the first sci-fi show “with a black Chosen One and a white Magical Negro.”

“The heyday of Twitter was during the Obama era. Now we’re living through the second Trump administration. Having a place to laugh to keep from crying is just as important as it ever was,” Jamilah Lemieux, a cultural critic and author who has 208,000 followers on the Meta-run platform, tells WIRED.

Lemieux was active on Twitter for over a decade, where she discussed motherhood and women’s rights, but started to pull back because the level of harassment and vitriol she was getting started to outweigh her positive interactions.

Twitter entered a new era, with a pointedly different vibe, in 2022 after Elon Musk bought the platform and renamed it X. For day-one users, the app was less functional: It was harder to see the content you wanted, hate speech and propaganda accounts surged, and moderation seemed to disappear overnight. “I’m not surprised that that happened. It was a very deliberate shift away from the progressive Black voices that had defined the platform for its earlier history,” says Lemieux, who describes the current experience of posting on X as “screaming into the void.”

Lemieux has since decamped to Threads, where she has become a power user of sorts, riffing on everything from singer Chris Brown to public versus private education. “I wanted a social media home again, but I just wasn't really sure where I fit. I have always preferred text to video in terms of the creation. And Threads offered what I loved about Twitter, which is that I could reach people with my words without having to curate visuals.”

Today, some of the biggest cultural voices on X have migrated to Threads—from author Roxane Gay and activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham to journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, whose recent New York Times Magazine essay about her decision to enroll her daughter in low-performing, predominantly Black public schools sparked an intense debate online around using your child to fight systemic failures.

“omg the threads convo about that article is better because NHJ is on there replying to ppl, god all the employed ppl really did go to threads,” TV writer @theashleyray posted on X, telling another user, “black twitter is there.”

Bluesky, which launched as invite-only in 2023 before opening up to the wider public a year later, initially announced itself as one of the first serious alternatives to X. But it wasn’t until Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential win that millions of users, seemingly in need of a public sphere free of the MAGA-fueled rhetoric that had overtaken the platform, flocked to Bluesky. They were eager to recapture the spirit of social media’s prime years.

Emboldened by its decentralized format and the promise of improved user safety mechanisms, Rudy Fraser, a developer with a background in community organizing, created Blacksky, a custom feed and moderation service that quickly became a central meeting ground for many Black users on the platform. It has proven to be a more secure social ecosystem for Black users, but it hasn’t exactly swayed public discourse in the way Black Twitter did with #OscarsSoWhite or #IfTheyGunnedMeDown.

Part of that is a numbers game, says Rianna Walcott, an assistant professor of communication at the University of Maryland who founded the Black Digital Migration Project, a research initiative examining how Black social media users respond to changing platform conditions.

“The problems of platform fatigue and reaching a globally Black audience are probably limiting Blacksky’s visibility, as it lacks the initial buy-in that comes from an already connected platform ecosystem like Meta’s,” Walcott says. In the beginning, Bluesky’s biggest user base was concentrated among progressives, particularly journalists, academics, activists, and writers. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 69 percent of respondents who were left-leaning news influencers joined the platform during its first year. And while Blacksky was fundamental to the platform’s nascent growth, Black engagement has stalled for a number of reasons; several colleagues and friends of mine stopped using it after the first few months, seemingly disheartened by its low-key atmosphere, on top of having to rebuild their social media presence in a new corner of the internet.

Threads, meanwhile, prioritizes engagement and allows users to easily join communities like Black Threads, Black British Threads, or Black LGBTQ Threads that are tailor-fit to their interests. According to a Meta blog post from December, there are over 200 groups, which include everything from TV and fitness to the NBA.

“I think it matters more to Black users where they can find each other at volume rather than the overall politics of the platform,” says Walcott.

While Spill, the image-forward social media network launched by Alphonzo Terrell, a former Twitter employee, has been successful in directly appealing to Black people, Threads has a unique advantage when it comes to onboarding new members because of its tight integration with Facebook and Instagram, platforms that have over 6 billion users combined. Threads has more than 500 million monthly active users and, in terms of sheer capacity, is on track to surpass X’s 557 million monthly active users, according to a Statista report from March.

Lemieux appreciates how seamless the platform is compared to X. “We often joke that Threads will drop you off anywhere,” she says. “A lot of the laughter and humor, it’s not just Black people coming up with hashtags like it was before, sometimes it’s just a middle-aged white woman’s Facebook post, who has cross-posted to Threads without realizing it.”

Though many of the same people and conversations that defined Black Twitter have moved to Threads, “Black Threads doesn’t feel like an exact replica of Black Twitter to me,” says Phil Lewis, an editor at HuffPost and news aggregator. He says that Black Twitter especially “shined” when users live-tweeted events, like award shows and sports events. “I haven’t seen that yet. But you can feel when a cultural moment is happening on Threads in the same way.”

Even so, the platform has been able to move the needle in surprising ways. In August, when the majority-Black city of Gary, Indiana, lost power for two weeks, causing a food shortage, among a long list of other safety concerns, Lewis says it was users on TikTok and Threads who first raised awareness about the historic blackout, which had received very little national media coverage until that point. “Then news outlets started paying attention.”

One of the most striking things Walcott has noticed about Threads as the spiritual successor to Black Twitter is how users are deliberately building and maintaining a narrative of its history. “People talk about events in Threads history like they did and do with Black Twitter,” she says. “When something happens that calls for comment, people turn to Threads for that discourse, just as they once turned to Twitter as the center of a hypernarrative web.”

User @missglowdigger certainly agrees. “Threads is single handedly thee best thing to happen to black social media,” she posted in September.

To which she was swiftly reminded: “Yes it is and I love the community BUT let us not get too comfortable … this is still a White Mans app.”

entries.title: How Israeli Checkpoints Choke Palestinian Life in the Occupied West Bank
entries.summary: Lost time. Lost jobs. Lost friends. Lost family. Lost lives. Our joint investigation reveals the system that has divided the West Bank and measures what it cost people to move through it.
entries.content:
Aref Jaber is on a neighbor's roof, trying to get home.

At 51, he is clambering over a wall into the next backyard, up onto the next roof, along the line of stone houses that stand between him and his own front door. He has no choice. Alleys and side streets in his neighborhood have been sealed with cement blocks and barbed wire, and a single point of access, called Checkpoint 160, is the only way in or out for the 140 families who live there.

But Checkpoint 160 is closed again; Jaber is not sure why. The whim of a soldier, a crash in the scanning system, breaking news in the region—it could be anything.

For the last three years, he says, this has happened at least two days a week. So the community has devised a system of alternative routes. Jaber calls his neighbors to ask if he can come through. They check their windows for soldiers, and then Jaber scales ladders and traverses roofs. “When I finally get home,” he says, “it feels like I’ve achieved something monumental.”

The enclosure of Jaber’s neighborhood is a dense microcosm of what life is becoming across the occupied West Bank—for Palestinians, that is. At the same time that deadly Israeli settler violence robs communities in the West Bank of their land, and amid the genocide in Gaza, Israel has expanded its infrastructures of military control and domination.

Since 2023, Israel’s fragmentation of Palestine, underway for generations, has accelerated. The West Bank has, for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians who live there, ceased to exist as a contiguous territory. According to the most recent UN data from December 2025, at least 925 fixed and temporary checkpoints, metal gates, roadblocks, and earth mounds divide the West Bank. (A Palestinian governmental commission reported this month that the number is now 942.) This fracturing has torn families apart, stifled the economy, and obstructed access to essential services such as hospitals and schools.

entries.title: Best Mattresses for Kids (2026): Saatva, Birch, Helix, and More
entries.summary: Learn what to look for when buying a kids’ mattress, plus how six top models stack up, according to my 2-year-old.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Kids, especially toddlers, aren’t mattress reviewers. They don’t wake up and tell you the pressure relief is lacking or that they appreciated the vegan foam and airy woven top. Instead, as a parent, it’s your job to become the observer, paying attention to the little things, like how easily they can climb into bed, whether they stay asleep, if they seem comfortable while moving around, plus how well the mattress can handle inevitable spills, jumping, and tumbling.

For the last few months, my toddler daughter tested each mattress in this guide in her bedroom on a Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. I narrowed down the mattresses tested by looking for beds specifically designed for children and prioritizing a mix of constructions, price points, and features. I paid close attention to everything from how well she slept, how easily she could climb onto the mattress, the edge support for myself during bedtime stories, and how cool each cover felt on a warm summer day. Some mattresses stood out for specific features, while others offered impressive value or the ability to grow with your child. Regardless of the specific accolade, every pick here earned its spot through toddler testing.

Want more mattress-buying advice for every kind of sleeper? Check out our guide to the Best Mattresses, the Best Organic Mattresses, and the Best Mattresses for Side Sleepers.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Also Tested

Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress for $919 (Twin): My biggest complaint with the Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress is, unfortunately, the reason I had to stop testing it. It was just short enough that it didn’t fit in my daughter’s twin bed frame, leaving a solid 8-inch gap between the bottom edge of the mattress and the foot of the bed frame. Every other twin mattress I tested fit the frame without any issues, making the Nolah the odd one out. It’s a bummer, because the mattress otherwise had a lot going for it. It’s got the flippability of many mattresses we tested, and its hybrid design was very comfy, with great edge support. If it’d fit the bed frame properly, I think it would’ve been a contender.

FAQs

What’s the Difference Between a Kids’ Mattress and a Regular Adult Mattress?

Many kids’ mattresses have firmer sleep surfaces for younger children and specific features like flippable designs, waterproof and stain-resistant covers, or reinforced edges that stand up to roughhousing. Kids’ mattresses also typically have a lower profile, which makes it easier and safer for kids to get in and out of bed.

They’re also available in smaller sizes, most commonly twin and full, which are typical for kids’ bedrooms and smaller bed frames. A full-size mattress can make sense for a child who needs more room but still benefits from the features mentioned above. Once your child reaches their teen years or no longer needs these features, an adult mattress may make more sense.

Why Are Many Kids’ Mattresses Flippable?

Many kids’ mattresses are designed to grow with your child. They typically have a firmer side for younger children as they transition from a crib mattress and a softer side for older kids. Being able to adjust firmness by flipping the mattress can save you from replacing it after a few years when your kid’s wants change.

What Do Mattress Certifications Mean?

You’ll probably come across several mattress certifications while shopping. Here’s what the most common ones mean:

  • CertiPur-US applies to polyurethane foam and verifies that the foam has been independently tested for emissions, durability, and certain chemicals, including formaldehyde and specific flame retardants.
  • GreenGuard Gold certifies that a mattress has been tested for low chemical emissions, known as volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which can cause irritation in the nose, eyes, throat, as well as other ailments.
  • Global Organic Latex Standard (GOLS) verifies that latex is responsibly sourced and processed according to environmental and production standards.
  • Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) certifies organic textile materials like cotton and wool. It ensures the materials meet strict environmental and manufacturing standards, with no VOC emissions or off-gassing.

We have more info about mattress shopping terms.

Should I Buy a Foam or Hybrid Mattress for My Child?

Foam mattresses are usually lighter and easier to move, which helps when you’re changing sheets or rotating the mattress. Hybrid mattresses combine foam with coils, which can boost pressure relief, edge support, and airflow to help prevent overheating. Neither is inherently better; it comes down to your little one’s needs and what feels most comfortable.

How Long Does a Kids’ Mattress Last?

A quality kids’ mattress should last anywhere from 7 to 10 years, depending on how heavily it’s used. Replace a mattress if you notice sagging, permanent body impressions, or tears. Also, if your child has outgrown the mattress’s size, it’s probably time for a new one.

What Should You Look for in a Mattress?

  • Materials: Kids’ mattresses use many of the same materials as adult mattresses. You’ll commonly see memory foam for cushioning, higher-density foam for support, latex for a responsive, bouncy feel, and steel coils for extra support, airflow, and edge support. You’ll also see materials like Tencel, which is a plant-based fiber often used in mattress covers because it’s soft and breathable. Cotton and wool are often found in natural or organic mattresses. When researching mattresses, you might also see materials described with the brand’s proprietary names, whether it's gel-infused memory foam or a stain-resistant treatment. When shopping for and comparing mattresses, look past the marketing name to see what the material actually is and what purpose it serves.
  • Firmness: There’s not much strong research or official medical guidance on mattress firmness for children. However, the American Academy of Pediatrics does specify that infants should sleep on a firm, flat mattress to reduce the risk of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID). When it comes time to transition out of the crib and into a “big kid bed,” it stands to reason that a firmer mattress will be more comfortable and familiar to a young child. Mattress firmness for kids of any age is ultimately a matter of preference, not a medical mandate, but we recommend consulting your child’s pediatrician for additional advice.
  • Pressure Relief: A mattress that properly supports a child’s weight can help with body development and spinal alignment as they grow. It can also help prevent restless nights and lead to better sleep.
  • Edge Support: This refers to how reinforced a mattress’s perimeter is. As a parent who loves reading with my daughter, the last thing I want is for the mattress edge to sink in as I sit next to her. It also helps protect a child from falling out of the bed.
  • Shipping, Trial, Warranty: Most online mattresses ship compressed in a box and are delivered directly to your door, and some brands offer in-home delivery and setup. A sleep trial gives you a window to test the mattress at home and return it if it isn’t a good fit. Be sure to pay attention to the fine print, though; some brands charge return or processing fees. The warranty covers manufacturing defects for a set period but typically not normal wear and tear, spills, or damage.
  • What Else to Consider: Be sure the mattress fits your child’s bed frame. Also consider the height, especially if the mattress will be used on bunk beds and trundles. If you’re hoping to keep a mattress for several years, a flippable model can offer more flexibility. Also consider the practical stuff: stain-resistant and water-repellent covers can come in handy for inevitable spills or accidents.

Should I Buy a Mattress in a Store or Online?

All of the mattresses I tested for this guide were purchased online, and most were shipped vacuum-sealed in a box. Many come with sleep trials so you can test them at home and return them if they don’t work for you.

Buying online often makes it easier to compare prices, materials, and certifications without driving from store to store. That said, shopping in person lets you get a sense of a mattress’s firmness before committing.

How I Tested

My almost 2-year-old daughter tested each mattress in her own bedroom over several months, sleeping on them in the same Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. Because toddlers don’t provide detailed feedback on things like lumbar support and motion transfer, I took a more observational approach by paying attention to how well she seemed to sleep and how easily she could climb into bed.

I also tested each mattress from a parent’s perspective by sitting on the edges, climbing into the beds for nighttime cuddles, and monitoring things like how easy it was to set up, whether my daughter seemed hot while sleeping/after waking up, how supportive it felt, and how the mattress held up to normal toddler behavior. I also considered each mattress’s construction, materials, and price.

I narrowed down the mattresses by focusing on models designed and marketed for children rather than smaller versions of adult mattresses. I wanted to test a range of price points and constructions, as well as explore features relevant for kids, like flippable designs, stain resistance, and lower heights.

entries.title: The 6 Best Laptop Docking Stations to Unlock the Full Desktop Experience (2026)
entries.summary: Docking stations expand what your laptop can do, and I’ve been testing the best of the best to see which you should buy.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Laptops are ideal for getting work done when you're out and about, but if you need the functionality of a full workstation, being hunched over a small, flat keyboard can quickly get annoying. However, connecting your laptop to a secondary monitor, a mouse, and a comfier keyboard can turn your desk space into a nest of tangled cables. Not to mention that many of today's laptops are designed to be as thin as possible and don't have the ports you may need to connect some peripherals. That's when it's time to get a laptop docking station.

Laptop docking stations are small boxes that sit on your desk and stay connected to your monitor (or monitors) and peripherals such as speakers, a keyboard, or a mouse. With the right docking station, you can enjoy the portability of a laptop with the flexibility and features of a desktop. These stations can get expensive, though, and it's hard to figure out which to buy based on a list of ports or specs. I've tested many of the most popular options and whittled the list down to the best laptop docking stations for various use cases.

Be sure to check out our other home office guides, including the Ultimate Work-From-Home Gear, Best USB Hubs, Best Office Chairs, Best Flash Drives, and Best Portable External Storage Drives.

Updated August 2026: I've added three new docks I've tested—the Baseus Spacemate Air 12-in-1, Belkin Connect Pro Thunderbolt 4 Dock, and the Belkin Connect USB-C GaN Dock. I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Other Laptop Docking Stations to Consider

We test a lot of laptop docking stations and, quite frankly, most of them are … fine. They're fine! We get into the nitty-gritty for specific use cases to find the best, but that leaves a bunch of devices that are great options even if they don't make our top picks. Here's a selection of some of our favorites, past favorites, or just alternatives to our picks above.

Baseus Spacemate Air 12-in-1 Mac Docking Station for $200: This is a really great budget option to the Plugable 5-Display USB-C dock above. While that one offers a faster and more full-featured way to get extra external displays, the Spacemate Air 12-in-1 gives you two 4K displays. That's especially helpful if you own an older MacBook Air or just appreciate the ease of use of connecting all your peripherals, displays, and accessories over a single USB-C cable. But I don't love the integrated cable; there are no card slots, and some of the USB ports aren't very fast.

Belkin Connect Pro Thunderbolt 4 Dock for $300: This one is a bit expensive for a Thunderbolt 4 dock, but it gets you 12 ports, including support for up to two 4K displays at 60 Hz and 90 watts of power delivery to your laptop. Like the Spacemate Air, it also includes some slower USB-A ports, though.

Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Pro Hub for $200: Sometimes, simpler is better. This docking station from Satechi is small, made of sturdy aluminum, and comes with just three Thunderbolt 4 ports on the rear, each of which is capable of up to 40 Gbps. Nothing else. This layout is surprisingly clean, with only a few cables coming out of the back, and one running to your laptop. If all you need is to connect to a couple of monitors or high-speed data storage and you like to keep your desk free of clutter, this is a great option. —Eric Ravenscraft

Satechi Triple 4K Docking Station for $300: Satechi's Triple 4K Docking Station supports three monitors, and while the first display output is HDMI-only, the two others can be connected via either HDMI or DisplayPort. Each display supports up to 4K resolution at 60 Hz, which is more than enough for most office or media work, though don't expect it to support the high frame rates you might want for gaming. —Eric Ravenscraft

Kensington Triple Video Mobile Dock for $90: A mobile docking station might sound like a contradiction, but in the case of the tiny Kensington Triple Video Mobile Dock, it makes a lot of sense. Using the included two HDMI ports and the DisplayPort, this little device can power three 1080p displays or two 4K displays—all at 60 Hz. It also has a USB-C port with 85 watts of pass-through charging, which is enough to charge most laptops. The downside is that it only supports a single 4K monitor on MacBooks, as the dual 4K support is only for Windows devices.

Satechi Dual Docking Station and Stand for $170: It's tough for laptop docking stations to stand out—most of them are simple boxes that add extra ports to your laptop—but Satechi's Dual Docking Station and Stand breaks the mold. It sits neatly under your laptop and elevates it slightly, putting it at an angle that has better ergonomics. A collection of three USB ports and three monitor output ports on the rear are conveniently placed so your desktop setup can stay connected while cables are tucked out of the way. A hardware switch on the back lets you turn the dock on or off. There's also a small strip of rubber on top and a built-in NVMe solid-state drive. While no SSD is included, you can plug in your own (something like this will work) to give your dock storage to offload files from your laptop.—Eric Ravenscraft

Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 Dock for $460: Sonnettech’s Echo 13 was one of the first Thunderbolt 5 docks out on the market. As it turns out, it's also one of the most unique offerings out there, including just about every port imaginable as well as an integrated M.2 storage slot with a Kingston SSD inside. While handy, I don't like that the drive isn't user accessible. The cheap plastic chassis is disappointing for the price, too.

Ivanky FusionDock Max 1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station for $330: It's hard to overstate how excessively luxurious this dock is. It's specifically for MacBook Pro users and can tackle up to four 6K screens, something only recent MacBook Pros support. The Ivanky FusionDock Max 1 accomplishes this via four USB-C Thunderbolt 4 ports, each capable of 40 Gbps data transfer speeds. If you're building the beefiest media workstation you can for the most powerful MacBook Pros on the market, this is it. Just put it on the company card, because it's expensive. —Eric Ravenscraft

Ugreen Revodok Max 213 Thunderbolt 4 for $300: Few people need an 8K display—or multiple 4K displays—but those who do know how difficult it can be to find gear that supports one. Fortunately, the Revodok Max 213 from Ugreen fits that bill. The DisplayPort 1.4 port can handle up to an 8K display at 30 Hz. It also comes with a Thunderbolt 4 upstream port that runs to your laptop, and, more importantly, a pair of downstream Thunderbolt 4 ports, which is another rarity among the docks I've tested. If you need to transfer a ton of media from various sources into one machine, connected to seriously high-res displays, this is the dock that can handle it all. —Eric Ravenscraft

Do You Need a Docking Station or a USB Hub?

This is the big question you'll want to answer before moving forward. Chances are you know if you need a full-on docking station rather than just a USB hub, but I'll explain the differences in case you're on the fence. A simple USB hub will handle most people's needs, as it will expand the potentially very limited ports of your laptop. If you own a MacBook Air, for example, a USB hub functions as a multiport adapter to get you HDMI, USB-A, and more. They're intended to be portable, and many of these hubs even include HDMI to connect an external display.

A laptop docking station will do quite a lot more. These devices are meant to be stationary on a desk, enabling you to access your entire workstation setup with just a single USB-C cable. The docking station is meant to stay put and have all your monitors and accessories plugged into it. Because of that, they require significantly more power and are often bundled with a large power brick. They are often quite expensive. So, while both accessories connect your laptop to more ports, they serve two different functions.

There are now lots of docks and hubs that blur the lines, offering multi-monitor support in a very small package. These can be useful, but a full docking station will still give you the fastest transfer speeds, the most ports, and better external display support all through a single cable.

What Ports Should Your Docking Station Have?

Figuring out the right connections you need for your setup can be daunting, and the confusing, arcane USB terminology only makes it worse. You can check out our explainer on parsing USB terms here. For the short version, here are the basics you should keep in mind:

Check your ports' speeds, and don't rely on version numbers. For a lot of confusing reasons, ports labeled as USB 3.0, 3.1, and 3.2 can all have the same speed or wildly different speeds. For this reason, docking station manufacturers have recently started opting to add speeds (usually written like “5 Gbps”) directly onto individual ports. Use the faster ports for transferring data, and slower ports for things like your keyboard and mouse.

Thunderbolt is best for lightning-fast data transfers or high-res displays. Thunderbolt is like a supercharged version of USB, and it even uses USB-C ports. However, Thunderbolt ports are also capable of transferring massive amounts of data. This makes it ideal for tasks like moving uncompressed video files around, as well as 4K (or even 8K) displays or lower-resolution monitors with extra high refresh rates.

Keep in mind your power needs. Most laptop docking stations will have some form of power connector and USB Power Delivery (or USB-PD) that can send power through to your laptop. You'll also sometimes see this referred to as “pass-through charging.” Most devices you connect will require their own power as well, especially if you want to connect monitors or charge your phone and tablet. If you plan to connect a lot of power-hungry devices, make sure your docking station can handle your needs.

Upstream and downstream ports. You'll often see USB ports labeled either as upstream or downstream. The data either flows up to the source (your PC or docking station) or down from the source. An upstream USB port means it's meant for transferring data from a peripheral (like an external drive) to your PC, whereas a downstream USB port only works in the opposite direction.

Mac-Compatible Docks

All the docks in our recommendations are compatible with both Mac and Windows, unless otherwise noted. But there are lots of hubs and docks out there that have certain limitations on Mac, such as only supporting mirroring mode in dual monitors. That's not a problem on Windows.

On lower-end Macs, there is a limitation on the number of screens. There is a way around this if you use a dock that supports DisplayLink. This software can create a “virtual GPU” that tricks the system into allowing for additional displays so you can drive more displays than are typically allowed on a MacBook Air, for example. In my experience, however, the performance can be shoddy, and you may run into issues with latency.

Is Thunderbolt 5 Worth It?

The first Thunderbolt 5-capable PCs, docks, and accessories came out in 2024. Thunderbolt 5 can now handle three 4K displays at 144 Hz (or two 4K displays at 240 Hz) and can deliver up to 240 watts of power. That's dramatic, up from the 100 watts of Thunderbolt 4. Thunderbolt 5 allows you to fully juice up more powerful devices, such as gaming laptops or the 16-inch M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Thunderbolt 5 docks are all backward compatible, so there's no worry about outdoing the peripherals you currently own. As is true in many scenarios, buying the latest specs is often worth it to avoid having to upgrade later. However, the adoption of Thunderbolt 5 has been slower than I'd hoped. And if you don't have a Thunderbolt 5 laptop to connect to, you won't get the full benefit that Thunderbolt 5 offers.

While there's a breadth of Thunderbolt 5 docks out in the world (many of which you'll see on this list), the biggest disappointment has been in the lack of Thunderbolt 5 accessories. It's still very difficult, for example, to find a Thunderbolt 5 SSD to achieve those faster speeds. Thunderbolt 5 docks are sometimes only marginally more expensive than previous-generation options, so they're often worth buying for the improved display support or higher power delivery. For example, CalDigit's TS5 is only $20 more than the TS4.

The EOS R50 V Body features an interchangeable lens for video shooting, with a redesigned user interface that includes a Vertical Video tripod mount and Front Record button—perfect for content creators of all types. Plus, there’s “Slow and Fast mode” for more creative control over the video frame rate and playback speed, along with dual pixel CMOS AF II tracking with “Register People Priority” and “Auto People, Animal, and Vehicle Subject Detection.” And even if you’re a novice, there are easy-to-use automatic exposure and scene modes like “movie,” for close-up demo, smooth skin, movie mode, and color filters.

Platinum is next, at $300 per year, and it offers 30% off repairs on up to 15 products and maintenance covered on 10 products. The top level is Cinema, which costs $1,000 per year and offers 30% off repairs on up to 20 products and maintenance covered on up to 10 products.

If you’re a photography pro, Canon even has an entire deals section for you. This section features exclusive discounts and better price drops than those available to regular customers. Expect the steepest discounts when you buy a lens kit and an EOS camera together, with discounts up to $1,600 off. Canon Professional Service discounts also extend to students over 18 years old—with no annual fee or points required to sign up. With the Canon Professional Service Student Membership, you can get a 10% discount on repairs for up to 2 products and a 10% discount on one Canon product per year.

Save Up to $1,000 Off With Canon Refurbished Discounts

The phrase stands true—Reduce, Reuse, Recycle—even for cameras. You can snag extra discounts on cameras this week with coupons on certified refurbished models—from $100 off to $900 off. For example, the refurbished EOS R5 Mark II Body is discounted by $271. There’s also the refurbished EOS R3 Body, now $900 off; the EOS R6 Mark II Body, for over $400 off; and the refurbished EOS R7 Body, priced at $1,119 with $80 off. All of these discounted Canon items are certified by Canon and come with a one-year limited warranty for added peace of mind.

Their refurbished selection is an awesome way to save tons of money—plus, these cameras are basically indistinguishable from new models. And since they have different restock schedules, you’ll have a better chance of scoring some of their most coveted models, like a Canon EOS Rebel T7 or Powershot G7 X.

Score up to $400 Off With Coupons for Canon Printers and Ink

entries.title: Fanatics Promo Code: 10% Off
entries.summary: Gear up for the season with verified Fanatics coupons, free shipping codes, and student or military discounts on jerseys, hats, and team gear.
entries.content:
Using a Fanatics promo code is one of the easiest ways to save this football season. If you’re a fan, you know Fanatics. Whether you’re shopping for your favorite team’s jersey for the next big game, looking for signed decor to display at home, or searching for a great gift for the fan in your life, Fanatics is the place to shop for sports team-themed apparel, sports gear, official team jerseys, authentic autographed memorabilia, and more.

Being a sports fanatic can be expensive, especially when you’re shopping for high-end official team gear. That’s why we offer a rotating selection of Fanatics coupons, including a Fanatics discount coupon for jerseys with free shipping, a Fanatics promo code for first-order savings, Fanatics coupons for military and first responders, and more to help your inner sports fanatic save.

Unlock a Fanatics Discount Coupon to Score Free Shipping

Shipping is often one of the highest hidden costs in online shopping. When you’re already spending so much on a custom-branded sports jersey, hoodie, or other gear, the last thing you want is another ten or twenty bucks in shipping fees. That’s why we offer a Fanatics discount coupon for jerseys with free shipping and a Fanatics coupon for Fanatics free shipping on jerseys. So, whether you want to rep your favorite team member from the NFL, NCAA, or F1, you’ll save. Use Fanatics coupon code GEARUP at checkout to get free shipping on select jerseys.

How to Use a Fanatics Coupon Code to Save 10%

One of the easiest ways to immediately save at Fanatics is to sign up for email and texts. Not only will you get the latest news on drops and collabs, exclusive discounts, and spotlights on rotating deals and limited-edition merch, you’ll also get a welcome email with a Fanatics promo code for 10% off your first purchase when you sign up for email and texts. It’s a super easy way to save initially without making extra purchases.

Make the Most of Fanatics One for 50% Off Tickets

If you’re an avid fan who often shops for sports memorabilia, it’s a great idea to become a Fanatics One member. You can sign up for a free membership, and your status will progress as you shop, play, and collect across the Fanatics website and store. The base membership is free and open to everyone. All you need to do is sign up, and you’ll start earning right away—with no spend required. With the basic Fanatics membership, you’ll earn FanCash on eligible Fanatics activity, get free shipping on orders of $39 or more, and receive a birthday gift. Plus, you get free returns and access to exclusive product drops in the Fanatics app.

The next Fanatics tier is Member Pro, which unlocks the benefits outlined below when you spend over $250 per year. Not only will you get all of the perks discussed in the base membership, but you’ll also get 3% FanCash back on purchases and 50% off ticket fees in the Fanatics app. Exclusive experiences, Tier Milestone Rewards, and Access to the Fanatics One Shop are just some of the additional perks you’ll get with the Member Pro membership.

Stack Fanatics Promo Codes With Military Discounts for 15% Off

Fanatics wants to show appreciation for those who serve by offering a 15% discount code on all orders to active-duty military personnel, reservists, retired or disabled veterans, and their immediate families. Be sure to check the fine print and take advantage of these Fanatics coupons for military and first responders, including 15% off purchases.

Score the Best Fanatics Collectibles

If you’re a sports collector, Fanatics should be your first choice. Through the Fanatics app and Fanatics online, you can bid on exclusive signed memorabilia and game-used collectibles from Fanatics Auctions. This gives you access to everything collectors covet: autographed photos, balls, bats, pucks, and jerseys featuring your favorite player, team, or historical moment. Be sure to check out Fanatics collectibles to complete your collection.

Give More With Fanatics Gift Cards

If you’re looking for a gift for a teenage boy or the man who seems impossible to shop for, a Fanatics gift card can be a thoughtful option. The giftee receives a dollar amount to spend at Fanatics, where they can shop for a wide range of gifts from their favorite teams and leagues.
